claim: Rapid and high-fidelity phosphorylation of serine residues at positions 32 and 36 of IκBα by IKK2/β is critical for canonical NF-κB activation.
source: Rapid and high-fidelity phosphorylation of serine residues at positions 32 and 36 of IκBα by IKK2/β, a highly conserved prototypical Ser/Thr kinase in vertebrates, is critical for canonical NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational claim about IKK2 function.

claim: Human IKK2 is a dual-specificity kinase that autophosphorylates at a tyrosine residue proximal to the active site.
source: Here, we report that human IKK2 not only phosphorylates substrate serine residues and autophosphorylates its own activation loop, but also autophosphorylates at a tyrosine residue proximal to the active site and is, therefore, a dual-specificity kinase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and related figures demonstrating tyrosine autophosphorylation.

claim: Mutation of Y169 to phenylalanine renders IKK2 incapable of catalyzing phosphorylation at S32 within its IκBα substrate.
source: We observed that mutation of Y169, an autophosphorylatable tyrosine located at the DFG +1 (DLG in IKK1/α and 2) position, to phenylalanine renders IKK2 incapable of catalyzing phosphorylation at S32 within its IκBα substrate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E, 3F, and 3G showing reduced phosphorylation activity of the Y169F mutant.

claim: Mutation of K44 to methionine converts IKK2 to an enzyme that no longer catalyzes specific phosphorylation of IκBα at S32 or S36, but rather directs phosphorylation of IκBα at other residues.
source: We also observed that mutation of the phylogenetically conserved ATP-contacting residue K44 in IKK2 to methionine converts IKK2 to an enzyme that no longer catalyzes specific phosphorylation of IκBα at S32 or S36, but rather directs phosphorylation of IκBα at other residues.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C and 3D showing altered substrate specificity of the K44M mutant.

claim: There is evidence of a phospho-relay from autophosphorylated IKK2 to IκBα in the presence of ADP.
source: Lastly, we report evidence of a phospho-relay from autophosphorylated IKK2 to IκBα in the presence of ADP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5B and 5E showing phosphotransfer from phosphorylated IKK2 to IκBα in the presence of ADP.

claim: Autophosphorylation of tyrosine(s) in the activation loop and the conserved ATP-contacting K44 residue provide IKK2's signal-responsive substrate specificity.
source: These observations suggest an unusual evolution of IKK2, in which autophosphorylation of tyrosine(s) in the activation loop and the conserved ATP-contacting K44 residue provide its signal-responsive substrate specificity and ensure fidelity during NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental observations described in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: IKK2 phosphorylates two critical serine residues (S32 and S36) near the N-terminus of IκBα in response to inflammatory or pathogenic signaling cues.
source: In response to inflammatory or pathogenic signaling cues, the IKK2 subunit becomes activated via phosphorylation at two serine residues within its activation loop and subsequently phosphorylates two critical serine residues (S32 and S36) near the N-terminus of IκBα (Inhibitor of NF-κB α), marking the inhibitor protein for ubiquitin-dependent 26 S proteasome-mediated degradation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism in the field, supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: Mutation of IκBα residues S32 and S36 to phospho-ablative alanine converts it into a super-repressor of NF-κB that is incapable of being degraded in response to NF-κB signaling.
source: Mutation of IκBα residues S32 and S36 to phospho-ablative alanine converts it into a super-repressor of NF-κB that is incapable of being degraded in response to NF-κB signaling (Brown et al., 1995; Lin et al., 1995), highlighting the need for exquisite specificity of IKK2 in phosphorylating these two serines (DiDonato et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IKK2 fails to phosphorylate IκBα when S32 and S36 are mutated to threonine.
source: The IKK2 subunit fails to phosphorylate IκBα when S32 and S36 are mutated even to threonine, another phosphorylatable residue.
evidence: This demonstrates the high specificity of IKK2 for serine residues at these positions.

claim: Purified recombinant full-length IKK2 is autophosphorylated when incubated with ATP in the absence of NEMO in a time-dependent manner.
source: We observed that purified recombinant full-length IKK2 is autophosphorylated when incubated with ATP in the absence of NEMO in a time-dependent manner, and likely at multiple sites as indicated by the diffuse nature of the slower migrating phospho-IKK2 band (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: NEMO enhances the specificity of IKK2 autophosphorylation.
source: The autophosphorylated IKK2 produced a sharper band in the presence of NEMO – possibly reflecting enhanced specificity of phosphorylation (Figure 1D, left panel)
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of a sharper band in the presence of NEMO as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: NEMO does not alter the efficiency of IKK2 phosphorylation of its substrate IκBα.
source: although NEMO did not alter the efficiency of phosphorylation for its bona fide substrate IκBα (Figure 1D, right panel).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: IKK2 K44M mutant lacks both autophosphorylation and IκBα phosphorylation activities.
source: An in vitro kinase assay with a K44M mutant of IKK2 that lacks both its autophosphorylation and IκBα phosphorylation activities along with the native sequence IKK2 using γ-32P-ATP confirmed that phosphorylation of IKK2 was self-catalyzed and not due to a spurious contaminating kinase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: K44 is an ATP-contacting residue that is conserved across STYKs, including IKK2.
source: K44 is an ATP-contacting residue that is conserved across STYKs, including IKK2, and its mutation to methionine typically reduces or eliminates kinase activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about kinase structure and function.

claim: IKK-specific ATP-competitive inhibitor Inhibitor VII inhibits specific phosphorylation of S32/36 on IκBα and IKK2-autophosphorylation.
source: An in vitro kinase assay showing inhibition of specific phosphorylation of S32/36 on IκBα and IKK2-autophosphorylation performed in the presence of an IKK-specific ATP-competitive inhibitor, Calbiochem Inhibitor VII, further validates that phosphorylation of IKK2 is due to its own activity (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Deletion IKK2-EE constructs lacking the C-terminal serine-rich region display both autophosphorylation and substrate IκBα phosphorylation activities.
source: These deletion IKK2-EE constructs displayed both autophosphorylation and substrate IκBα phosphorylation activities (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The observed autophosphorylation of IKK2 lacking serines of the activation loop and the C-terminal segment suggests the existence of hitherto uncharacterized sites of autophosphorylation in IKK2.
source: The observed autophosphorylation of IKK2 lacking serines of the activation loop and the C-terminal segment suggested the existence of hitherto uncharacterized sites of autophosphorylation in IKK2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that IKK2 constructs lacking known phosphorylation sites still undergo autophosphorylation.

claim: IKK2 undergoes de novo autophosphorylation at tyrosine residues when incubated with Mg2+-ATP.
source: Indeed, we observed by western blot with anti-phosphotyrosine antibodies the unexpected de novo autophosphorylation of IKK2 at tyrosine residues (Figure 2A, middle panel) in addition to the previously reported autophosphorylation of activation loop serines (Figure 2A, upper panel) when full-length native sequence IKK2 was incubated with Mg2+-ATP for various amounts of time.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ATP-dependent tyrosine autophosphorylation of IKK2 is inhibited by IKK-specific inhibitor Inhibitor VII.
source: ATP-dependent tyrosine autophosphorylation was not observed in the presence of an IKK-specific inhibitor, Inhibitor VII (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: IKK2 K44M mutant does not undergo tyrosine autophosphorylation.
source: ATP-dependent tyrosine autophosphorylation was not observed...with the kinase inactivating IKK2 K44M mutant (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Tyrosine autophosphorylation of IKK2 is undetectable at urea concentrations greater than 1 M.
source: Additionally, autophosphorylation assays performed in the presence of urea revealed tyrosine autophosphorylation to be undetectable at urea concentrations greater than 1 M (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IKK2 activities toward S32 and S36 of IκBα and its own tyrosine residue(s) are affected similarly by both general and IKK-specific kinase inhibitors.
source: The fact that activities of IKK2 toward S32 and S36 of IκBα and its own tyrosine residue(s) were affected similarly by both general (AMPPNP and Staurosporine) and IKK-specific (MLN-120B, TPCA, Inhibitor VII; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) kinase inhibitors indicates that both activities occur in the same active site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple inhibitors affect both activities similarly, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The C-terminal NBD of IKK2 is not required for its autocatalytic dual specificity and phosphorylation of IκBα at S32 and S36 in vitro.
source: Using various truncated versions of IKK2, we further observed that the C-terminal NBD of IKK2 is not required for its autocatalytic dual specificity and in phosphorylating IκBα at S32 and S36 (Figure 2E) in vitro.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Constitutively active NBD-deficient IKK2 (IKK2Δ664EE) undergoes de novo autophosphorylation at tyrosine residues but not at serines.
source: Semi-quantitative assessment of phospho-Ser and phospho-Tyr residues on a constitutively active NBD-deficient IKK2 (IKK2Δ664EE) was performed by western blot with monoclonal anti-phosphoserine and anti-phosphotyrosine antibodies, which revealed de novo autophosphorylation at tyrosine residues but not at serines (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The phospho-ablative S177A/S181A mutant of IKK2 lacks tyrosine autophosphorylation activity.
source: The phospho-ablative S177A/S181A (AA; non-phosphorylatable activation loop) mutant of IKK2, which is incapable of phosphorylating S32 and S36 of IκBα (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), also lacked tyrosine autophosphorylation activity (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Phosphorylation of activation loop S177/S181 is critical for dual specificity of IKK2.
source: in an in vitro kinase assay, suggesting that phosphorylation of activation loop S177/S181 is critical for dual specificity of IKK2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the S177A/S181A mutant lacks tyrosine autophosphorylation activity.

claim: Y169 was identified as the prominent tyrosine autophosphorylation site in IKK2 by mass spectrometric analyses.
source: We performed mass spectrometric analyses on in vitro autophosphorylated IKK2 and identified Y169 to be the prominent tyrosine autophosphorylation site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the active state conformers, the position and conformation of Tyr169 appears to be well positioned for accepting a phosphate from ATP intramolecularly.
source: In the active state conformers, the position and conformation of Tyr169 appears to be well positioned for accepting a phosphate from ATP intramolecularly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of IKK2 crystal structures as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The hydroxyl of Tyr169 in IKK2 projects toward the γ-phosphate of ATP similarly to the serine hydroxyl on the PKA inhibitor pseudo-substrate.
source: A superposition of IKK2 with a pseudo-substrate-bound PKA shows that the hydroxyl of Tyr169 in IKK2 projects toward the γ-phosphate of ATP similarly to the serine hydroxyl on the PKA inhibitor pseudo-substrate (Knighton et al., 1991; Nolen et al., 2004; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with PKA as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The position occupied by Y169 in IKK2 primary sequence corresponds to the classic DFG +1 position.
source: Interestingly, the position occupied by Y169 in IKK2 primary sequence corresponds to the classic DFG +1 (DLG in cases of IKK2 and IKK1; Figure 3A & B).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and structural analysis as shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The DFG +1 position has been reported to be critical in defining the substrate specificity of a kinase.
source: The DFG +1 position has been reported to be critical in defining the substrate specificity of a kinase (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: IKK2 K44M mutant retains weak autophosphorylation activity but more robust phosphorylation of full-length IκBα.
source: Surprisingly, IKK2 K44M displayed very weak (compared to that of WT IKK2) autophosphorylation activity but a more robust phosphorylation of full-length IκBα, albeit to a much lesser degree than native sequence IKK2, in a radioactive in vitro kinase assay (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: IKK2 K44M lacks phosphorylation of IκBα at S32 and S36.
source: Interestingly, we observed a lack of phosphorylation of IκBα at S32 and S36 by IKK2 K44M (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IKK2 K44M phosphorylates IκBα at residues within its C-terminal PEST region.
source: This suggests that IKK2 K44M phosphorylates IκBα at residues within its C-terminal PEST, consistent with the observed phosphorylation of IκBα (Figure 3C & D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that IKK2 K44M phosphorylates IκBα but not at S32/S36.

claim: IKK2 K44M phosphorylated super-repressor IκBα S32A/S36A more efficiently than native sequence IκBα.
source: Moreover, IKK2 K44M phosphorylated super-repressor IκBα S32A/S36A more efficiently than native sequence IκBα, in sharp contrast to IKK2 of native sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: IKK2 K44M retains significant kinase activity toward IκBα, although it is incapable of specific IκBα phosphorylation at S32, S36.
source: This suggests that IKK2 K44M retains significant kinase activity toward IκBα, although it is incapable of specific IκBα phosphorylation at S32, S36.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of IKK2 K44M activity.

claim: LC-MS/MS analysis of IKK2 K44M protein did not indicate the obvious presence of any contaminating kinase.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis with 20 μg of Sf9-derived IKK2 K44M protein used in our studies did not indicate the obvious presence of any contaminating kinase.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis to verify protein purity.

claim: An equivalent K to M mutant of Erk2 retained ~5% of its catalytic activity.
source: It is noteworthy that an equivalent K to M mutant of Erk2 retained ~5% of its catalytic activity (Robbins et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: IKK2 Y169F displays a severe reduction in both autophosphorylation and IκBα phosphorylation activities.
source: Next, we assessed the activity of a tyrosine-phosphoablative Y169F mutant of IKK2 in an in vitro kinase assay and observed a severe reduction in both autophosphorylation and IκBα phosphorylation activities (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: IKK2 Y169F displayed drastically reduced levels of kinase activity toward S36A/E mutants of IκBα.
source: IKK2 Y169F displayed drastically reduced levels of kinase activity toward S36A/E mutants of IκBα, while the S32A/E mutants were minimally affected when compared against the native IκBα substrate (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The tyrosine residue at position 169 might contribute toward signal-responsive phosphorylation of IκBα.
source: These observations suggest that the tyrosine residue at position 169 (and possibly its phosphorylation) might contribute toward signal-responsive phosphorylation of IκBα.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of the Y169F mutant.

claim: Catalytic activity is significantly reduced in IKK2 Y169F upon TNF-α treatment in ikk2-/- MEF cells reconstituted with IKK2 Y169F.
source: We also measured signal-induced activation of IKK2 upon TNF-α treatment in ikk2-/- mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cells reconstituted with native sequence IKK2 and IKK2 Y169F. Catalytic activity is significantly reduced in IKK2 Y169F (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Phosphorylation of activation loop serines was only marginally defective for IKK2 Y169F.
source: Nonetheless, phosphorylation of activation loop serines was only marginally defective for IKK2 Y169F as judged by anti-phosphoserine-177 western blot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Activation loop phosphorylation is necessary but not sufficient for IKK2 to become fully active.
source: hinting at the necessity, but not sufficiency, of activation loop phosphorylation for IKK2 to become fully active.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that IKK2 Y169F has normal activation loop phosphorylation but reduced activity.

claim: There is a possible interdependence of phosphorylation at Y169 of IKK2 and S32 of IκBα.
source: Together, these results imply a possible interdependence of phosphorylation at Y169 of IKK2 and S32 of IκBα.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of the Y169F mutant's effects on S32 phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation at S177 and S181 increased folding stability of IKK2, which was further stabilized by phosphorylation at Y169.
source: Phosphorylation at S177 and S181 increased folding stability of the kinase, which was further stabilized by phosphorylation at Y169 as evidenced by a gradual decrease in the total energy of the system (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Differential scanning calorimetry showed a change of Tm from ~40 °C to ~50 °C upon autophosphorylation of IKK2.
source: Results of differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) in the presence of ADP vs. ATP also indicated a change of Tm from ~40 °C to ~50 °C, reflecting a striking enhancement in stability upon autophosphorylation of IKK2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by DSC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased solubility of IKK2 upon autophosphorylation was found to be essential for its successful crystallization.
source: These results correlate with observations of increased solubility of IKK2 upon autophosphorylation; a property found to be essential for its successful crystallization (Polley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: P-IKK2 exhibited the highest RMSD, followed by p-IKK2, and then UnP-IKK2 in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Counter-intuitively, we observed the highest RMSD for P-IKK2, followed by p-IKK2, and then UnP-IKK2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The highest RMSD for P-IKK2 might be indicative of increased internal motion despite phosphorylation-induced stabilization.
source: This result might be indicative of increased internal motion despite phosphorylation-induced stabilization of IKK2 because of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RMSD data from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The glycine-rich loop and the αC-helix in p-IKK2 were positioned in a manner reminiscent of an active kinase.
source: We observed that, while the glycine-rich loop and the αC-helix in p-IKK2 were positioned in a manner reminiscent of an active kinase, those in UnP and P-IKK2 were oriented differently (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Helix αC was found to be distorted in P-IKK2 in a manner that would make it unlikely to support canonical phosphotransfer from ATP.
source: In fact, helix αC was found to be distorted in P-IKK2 in a manner that would make it unlikely to support canonical phosphotransfer from ATP.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The formation of the proper R- and C-spines in p-IKK2 confirmed its active conformation.
source: The formation of the proper R- and C-spines in p-IKK2 confirmed its active conformation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The p-IKK2 KD exhibited features consistent with an active kinase: a salt bridge between K44 and E61, and the 'DFG in' conformation.
source: The p-IKK2 KD exhibited additional features consistent with an active kinase: a salt bridge between K44 and E61 (K72 and E91 in PKA, respectively), and the 'DFG in' conformation (although the sequence is DLG in IKK2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: ATP binding to P-IKK2 is relatively unfavorable in both starting and ending structural models from molecular docking.
source: The results indicated that ATP binding to P-IKK2 is relatively unfavorable (docking score in positive range) in both starting and ending structural models (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is based on molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ADP binding is favorable for all phosphorylated or unphosphorylated IKK2 structural models except for the starting conformation of P-IKK2.
source: whereas ATP binding to UnP-IKK2 and p-IKK2 is favorable. ADP binding is, however, favorable for all phosphorylated or unphosphorylated IKK2 structural models except for the starting conformation of P-IKK2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ATP binding for the P-IKK2 population is highly unfavorable in contrast to their high relative preference for ADP.
source: We again observed that ATP binding for the P-IKK2 population is highly unfavorable in contrast to their high relative preference for ADP, whereas p-IKK2 displayed comparable preference for both ATP and ADP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on binding free energy calculations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In the ATP-docked structures, the terminal phosphate was in close proximity to the Y169-OH, consistent with the likelihood of autophosphorylation at Y169.
source: In the ATP-docked structures, the ATP phosphate groups exhibited a pose (ΔG=–10.64 kcal/mol) very similar to that observed in the PKA structure (PDB ID: 1ATP) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), and the terminal phosphate was in close proximity to the Y169-OH, consistent with the likelihood of autophosphorylation at Y169 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The presence of ATP enhanced the formation of the R- and C-spines in ATP-bound p-IKK2.
source: Further analyses of the ATP-bound p-IKK2 structure confirmed that the presence of ATP enhanced the formation of the R- and C-spines, as observed in active forms of kinases (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of ATP-bound p-IKK2 shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Narrowing of the canonical ATP-binding pocket in P-IKK2 may lead to rejection of ATP from the canonical binding pocket.
source: Superposition of the ATP from p-IKK2 on P-IKK2 indicated that narrowing of the canonical ATP-binding pocket in P-IKK2 may lead to rejection of ATP from the canonical binding pocket, triggered by severe clashes between the glycine-rich loop and ATP (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The R-spine in P-IKK2 exhibited a discontinuity, with M65 located away from the other three conserved spine residues.
source: Furthermore, the R-spine in P-IKK2 exhibited a discontinuity (Figure 4H), with M65 (L95 in PKA) located away from the other three conserved spine residues and from the glycine-rich loop.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: P-IKK2 is unable to accommodate ATP in a manner similar to that observed in experimentally determined kinase structures, but could accommodate ADP into the ATP-binding cleft comfortably.
source: The superposition of ADP (from the docked complex of p-IKK2 and ADP, ΔG=–9.88 kCal/mol, Figure 4I) onto the P-IKK2 structure confirmed that while P-IKK2 is unable to accommodate ATP in a manner similar to that observed in experimentally determined kinase structures, it could accommodate ADP into the ATP-binding cleft comfortably (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4I and 4J.

claim: The affinities of ATP and ADP for p-IKK2 appear comparable as indicated by their respective binding energy/docking score values.
source: The affinities of ATP and ADP for p-IKK2 appear comparable as indicated by their respective binding energy/docking score values, like in other kinases (Becher et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on docking analysis and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The cellular concentrations of ATP vs ADP could play an important role in kinase activity.
source: Thus, the cellular concentrations of ATP vs ADP could play an important role in kinase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparable affinities of ATP and ADP for p-IKK2.

claim: ADP-bound P-IKK2 could act as an intermediate to relay phosphates back to ATP or to substrates.
source: We speculate that ADP-bound P-IKK2, containing various and perhaps transiently phosphorylated groups within the activation loop and in close proximity to the active site, could act as an intermediate to relay phosphates back to ATP or to substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural and biochemical observations.

claim: Phosphorylation of tyrosine residue(s) in IKK2 was only observed upon ATP treatment of purified IKK2 proteins.
source: We observed phosphorylation of tyrosine residue(s) only upon ATP treatment of purified IKK2 proteins, hinting at the likelihood of efficient cellular phosphotyrosine phosphatases (Eckhart et al., 1979).
evidence: This is an observation from experiments and an inference about cellular phosphatases.

claim: Crystal structures of Sf9-derived human IKK2 did not indicate phosphates on tyrosine residues even though recombinant IKK2 was treated with Mg2+-ATP as part of the purification.
source: Surprisingly, crystal structures of Sf9-derived human IKK2 did not indicate phosphates on tyrosine residues even though recombinant IKK2 was treated with Mg2+-ATP as part of the purification (PDB ID: 4E3C; Polley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from structural data and supported by a citation.

claim: Phosphotyrosine residue(s) in IKK2 might serve as a transient sink of phosphate for its eventual transfer to ADP or serines in the IκBα substrate.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that phosphotyrosine residue(s) in IKK2 might somehow serve as a transient sink of phosphate for its eventual transfer to ADP or serines in the IκBα substrate.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observations about phosphotyrosine stability.

claim: Nucleotide-free autophosphorylated IKK2 can transfer radiolabeled phosphate to IκBα.
source: The nucleotide-free autophosphorylated IKK2 (P-IKK2) was then incubated with substrate IκBα either in the absence or with the fresh addition of unlabeled ATP/ADP. Resolution of the reaction mixture on an SDS-PAGE and subsequent autoradiography indicated transfer of radiolabeled phosphate to IκBα (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Transfer of radiolabeled phosphate from P-IKK2 to IκBα is significantly enhanced in the presence of cold ADP.
source: which was significantly enhanced in the presence of cold ADP (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of excess cold ATP did not reduce the extent of IκBα phosphorylation, strongly suggesting the transfer of 32P-phosphate from 32P-IKK2 to IκBα.
source: Addition of excess cold ATP did not reduce the extent of IκBα phosphorylation, strongly suggesting the transfer of 32P-phosphate from 32P-IKK2 to IκBα (Figure 5B) and consistent with an IKK2-mediated phosphate relay mechanism.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Autophosphorylated IKK2 obtained by treatment with excess cold ATP and purified by size-exclusion chromatography can transfer phosphate to IκBα substrate in the presence of ADP.
source: This P-IKK2 was incubated with IκBα substrate either in the presence or absence of ADP for varying time periods. A similar reaction was set up in the presence of ATP instead of ADP as a positive control. We observed, by western blot with sequence-specific anti-phosphoserine antibody, efficient phosphorylation of IκBα S32 and S36 residues in the presence of ADP (10 and 50 μM) but not in its absence. As anticipated, a robust phosphorylation of IκBα was observed in the presence of 50 μM ATP (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Phosphorylation of S32/S36 of IκBα increased with time in the phosphotransfer assay with ADP.
source: Next, we followed the same experimental scheme as shown in Figure 5C and assessed IκBα phosphorylation by relay mechanism at a finer time interval. Phosphorylation of S32/S36 of IκBα increased with time as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ESI-MS analysis of 50 μM ADP solution did not detect any peak corresponding to ATP.
source: The requirement for ADP in the observed phosphotransfer prompted us to consider if our ADP was contaminated with trace amounts of ATP. ESI-MS analysis of our 50 μM ADP solution did not detect any peak corresponding to ATP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Generation/presence of ATP could not be detected by TLC-based analysis in the phosphotransfer assay conditions.
source: Dependence of IκBα phosphorylation on ADP raises the possibility of infinitesimal reversibility generating ATP from ADP in the active site of the kinase. We could not detect the generation/presence of ATP in a setting similar to that described in Figure 5A & B by TLC-based analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Phosphotransfer from P-IKK2 is restricted to the S32 and S36 residues of IκBα and not directed toward serine/threonine residues within the C-terminal PEST domain.
source: We next tested whether the observed phosphotransfer to IκBα is restricted only to the S32 and S36 residues required for NF-κB activation or also directed toward serine/threonine residues within the C-terminal PEST domain of IκBα. Kinase assays performed with P-IKK2 and IκBα of native sequence or harboring S32A and S36A mutations (AA) in the presence of γ-32P-ATP revealed a lack of phosphorylation of IκBα AA, although that protein retains the serines and threonines of the C-terminal PEST region (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: IKK2-Y169F is unable to transfer phosphate to IκBα.
source: Furthermore, a similar assay with IKK2-Y169F showed its inability to transfer phosphate to IκBα (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transfer of phosphate from P-IKK2 to IκBα is exclusively to S32 and S36, likely from Y169.
source: Taken together, this hints at the transfer of phosphate exclusively to S32 and S36 of IκBα from Y169.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations with Y169F mutant and phosphotransfer assays.

claim: AMPPNP has no inhibitory effect on the phosphotransfer from P-IKK2 to IκBα, irrespective of the presence of ADP.
source: We also observed no inhibitory effect on the phosphotransfer by AMPPNP, an unhydrolyzable analogue of ATP, irrespective of the presence of ADP. This suggests that diverse adenine nucleotides prompt phosphotransfer by the kinase (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: IKK2 phosphorylates IκBα sequentially at S32 followed by S36 following a single binding event.
source: It is noteworthy that a recent study reported that IKK2 phosphorylates IκBα sequentially at S32 followed by S36 following a single binding event and that phosphorylation of S32 increases the phosphorylation rate of S36 (Stephenson et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Catalytically active IKK2 phosphorylated at S177 and S181 can undergo autophosphorylation on tyrosine residues within its activation loop.
source: Taken together with our results, we propose that catalytically active IKK2, that is by definition phosphorylated at S177 and S181, can undergo autophosphorylation on tyrosine residues within its activation loop.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tyrosine autophosphorylated IKK2 could serve as a phosphoenzyme intermediate to transfer its phosphate group to S32 of IκBα.
source: Furthermore, the tyrosine autophosphorylated IKK2 could serve as a phosphoenzyme intermediate to transfer its phosphate group to S32 of IκBα, thereby enhancing the rate of phosphorylation at S36, possibly using ATP for the second site phosphorylation at S36 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental results, illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: IKK2 is a dual-specificity kinase that phosphorylates serine residues on itself and on substrates, as well as tyrosine residues on itself.
source: These results demonstrate the dual specificity of recombinant IKK2 in phosphorylating serine residues on itself and on substrates, as well as tyrosine residues on itself.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: IKK2 activities toward S32 and S36 of IκBα and its own tyrosine residue(s) occur in the same active site.
source: The fact that activities of IKK2 toward S32 and S36 of IκBα and its own tyrosine residue(s) were affected similarly by both general (AMPPNP and Staurosporine) and IKK-specific (MLN-120B, TPCA, Inhibitor VII; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) kinase inhibitors indicates that both activities occur in the same active site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple inhibitors affect both activities similarly.

claim: IKK2 appears to be the only other metazoan protein kinase that derives its substrate specificity through the formation of a phosphoenzyme intermediate apart from MHCK of Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: So far, IKK2 appears to be the only other metazoan protein kinase that derives its substrate specificity through the formation of a phosphoenzyme intermediate apart from MHCK of Dictyostelium discoideum (an atypical eukaryotic protein kinase; Ye et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparative claim supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The transfer of phosphate from Tyr169 to Ser32 of IκBα represents an intriguing and unprecedented mechanism among metazoan protein kinases.
source: The transfer of phosphate from Tyr169 to Ser32 of IκBα represents an intriguing and unprecedented mechanism among metazoan protein kinases.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results and comparison with known kinase mechanisms.

claim: The hydroxyl group of Tyr169 is optimally positioned to readily accept the γ-phosphate from ATP at the expense of minimal energy.
source: We propose a possible explanation for the process: the hydroxyl group of Tyr169 is optimally positioned to readily accept the γ-phosphate from ATP at the expense of minimal energy in the presence or absence of the substrate IκBα.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural analysis.

claim: The relay of phosphate from ATP to Tyr169 to Ser32 might offer a more energetically favorable pathway than a direct transfer of phosphate from ATP to the substrate.
source: This relay of phosphate – from ATP to Tyr169 to Ser32 – might offer a more energetically favorable pathway than a direct transfer of phosphate from ATP to the substrate.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the energetics of the proposed mechanism.

claim: ADP or AMPPNP might act as an ATP surrogate in helping IKK2 adopt a conformational state commensurate with selective phosphorylation of S32 and S36 in IκBα.
source: Taken together, we surmise that ADP or AMPPNP might act as an ATP surrogate in helping IKK2 adopt a conformational state commensurate with selective phosphorylation of S32 and S36 in IκBα.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that AMPPNP does not inhibit phosphotransfer.

claim: A similar phenomenon of ADP acting as a potent stimulator is reported for IRE1.
source: A similar phenomenon is reported for IRE1, where ADP was found to be a potent stimulator of its ribonuclease activity, and AMPPNP was also reported as a somewhat effective potentiator (Lee et al., 2008; Sidrauski and Walter, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on IRE1.

claim: Ser32 cannot be efficiently phosphorylated by p-IKK2:ATP due to a deliberate chemical mismatch of the hydroxyl group of Ser32 within the active site.
source: We speculate that Ser32 cannot be efficiently phosphorylated by p-IKK2:ATP due to a deliberate chemical mismatch of the hydroxyl group of Ser32 within the active site. However, it aligns well with the P-IKK2:ADP intermediate.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the mechanism of substrate specificity.

claim: The amplitude, duration, and kinetics of IKK activity correlate with the strength of input signal, level of IκBα degradation, and NF-κB activation.
source: The amplitude, duration, and kinetics of IKK activity correlate with the strength of input signal, level of IκBα degradation, and NF-κB activation (Behar and Hoffmann, 2013; Cheong et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The digital activation profile of NF-κB may be intrinsically linked to the phosphorelay process.
source: This digital (all-or-none) activation profile of NF-κB appears to be due to rapid activation and inactivation of IKK2. The primary target of IKK2 is IκBα, which underlies the rapid activation of NF-κB, although multiple other substrates are targeted in vivo. This digital activation profile may be intrinsically linked to the phosphorelay process.
evidence: This is a speculative claim linking the phosphorelay mechanism to the digital activation profile.

claim: P-IKK2 transfers phosphate(s) efficiently and specifically to S32 and S36 of IκBα, but not to other phosphorylatable sites.
source: We observe that P-IKK2 transfers phosphate(s) efficiently and specifically to S32 and S36 of IκBα, but not to other phosphorylatable sites, such as the serine and threonine residues within the IκBα C-terminal PEST region (Figures 5B, E, 6A).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B, 5E, and 6A.

claim: The transiency of various phosphorylated residues in P-IKK2 could underlie the activation-inactivation event during signal response.
source: We surmise that the transiency of various phosphorylated residues in P-IKK2 could underlie the activation-inactivation event during signal response.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the functional significance of transient phosphorylation.

claim: Functional regulation of IKK2 might involve properties analogous to that of the two-component histidine kinase-effector systems.
source: In this context, it will be worth investigating if functional regulation of IKK2 involves properties analogous to that of the two-component histidine kinase-effector systems (Bhate et al., 2015; Lamarche et al., 2008; Laub and Goulian, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative claim suggesting future research directions, supported by citations.

claim: Phosphate transfer directly from phosphohistidine is energetically far more favorable than from phosphotyrosine, except in enzymatic processes.
source: It is noteworthy that phosphate transfer directly from phosphohistidine is energetically far more favorable than from phosphotyrosine, except in enzymatic processes.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about phosphate chemistry.

claim: The phosphotransfer from P-IKK2 to IκBα reflects a single turnover event in the absence of the phosphate donor, ATP.
source: The phosphotransfer from P-IKK2 to IκBα investigated and reported herein reflects a single turnover event in the absence of the phosphate donor, ATP (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental design and results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Not every phosphorylated residue over the long span of P-IKK2 is expected to have the ability to transfer its phosphate to IκBα.
source: Not every phosphorylated residue over the long span of P-IKK2 is expected to have the ability to transfer its phosphate to IκBα and additionally, the P-IKK2 likely represents a pool with a non-homogeneous distribution of phosphorylated residues.
evidence: This is an inference about the heterogeneity of the P-IKK2 population.

claim: The sub-stoichiometric phospho-relay could be due to non-homogeneous distribution of phosphorylated residues in P-IKK2.
source: This could be a reason for the observance of the sub-stoichiometric phospho-relay.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the observed sub-stoichiometric phosphotransfer.

claim: K44 plays a critical role in autophosphorylation of IKK2 and specific phosphorylation of S32 and S36 in IκBα.
source: We also observe a critical role of K44 in autophosphorylation of IKK2 and specific phosphorylation of S32 and S36 in IκBα.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results with the K44M mutant.

claim: A particular structural state of IKK2 or its interaction with a partner protein could direct IKK2 to phosphorylate specific sites within different substrates.
source: It is possible that a particular structural state of IKK2 or its interaction with a partner protein could direct IKK2 to phosphorylate specific sites within different substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the regulation of IKK2 substrate specificity.

claim: The activation of NF-κB through unique phosphorylation events catalyzed by IKK2 appears to be regulated by a complex and multi-layered fail-safe mechanism.
source: It is intriguing how the activation of NF-κB, through unique phosphorylation events catalyzed by IKK2, appears to be regulated by a complex and multi-layered fail-safe mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the overall findings of the study.

claim: In the absence of upstream signals, the IKK complex is unable to phosphorylate Ser 32/36 of IκBα efficiently.
source: In the absence of upstream signals, the IKK complex is unable to phosphorylate Ser 32/36 of IκBα efficiently, thereby keeping a check on the aberrant and untimely activation of NF-κB.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about IKK regulation.

claim: NEMO warrants IKK activation and ensures that the IKK complex specifically chooses IκBα from a large pool of substrates of IKK2.
source: NEMO warrants IKK activation and ensures that the IKK complex specifically chooses IκBα from a large pool of substrates of IKK2.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NEMO function.

claim: IKK2 is designed such that it phosphorylates itself at an activation loop tyrosine when activated, so that phosphate group(s) can be relayed directly to Ser32/36 of IκBα with great fidelity.
source: IKK2 is designed in such a manner that it phosphorylates itself at an activation loop tyrosine when activated, such that phosphate group(s) can be relayed directly to Ser32/36 of IκBα with great fidelity, thus leaving little chance of a misconstrued signaling event thereby confirming NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the proposed mechanism based on the study's findings.

claim: The discovery of phosphotransfer reaction in IKK2 could present the beginning of a new aspect in eukaryotic cell signaling by EPKs.
source: Our discovery of an intriguing phosphotransfer reaction that helps accomplish the desired specificity could present the beginning of a new aspect in eukaryotic cell signaling by EPKs.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the broader significance of the findings.
